themes.what: God calls on the house of David to act justly and warns of His anger if they do not.
God rebukes those who believe they are safe and untouched by enemies.
themes.words: מִי יֵחַת עָלֵינוּ, מִי יָבוֹא בִּמְעוֹנוֹתֵינוּ

themes.theme: Judgment on the Kings of Judah
themes.what: The chapter delivers a message of divine judgment against the kings of Judah, particularly those who fail to uphold justice and righteousness.
The chapter warns that oppression of the vulnerable and turning to other gods will lead to exile and disgrace.
The chapter condemns the pursuit of personal wealth and luxury without justice as a false form of success.

themes.theme: Exile and Disgrace of the Royal Line
themes.what: The chapter foretells the exile and disgrace of the royal family, including the burial of Jehoiakim like a donkey.
The chapter condemns corrupt leaders who have scattered and neglected God's people.
God promises to raise up a righteous ruler from David's line who will bring justice and peace.
The chapter denounces prophets who spread lies, take bribes, and mislead the people.
God declares judgment on those who have ignored or misrepresented His word.
God asserts His omnipresence and authority over all things, including the false claims of prophets.
God distinguishes between the exiles in Babylon and those who remained in Judah, showing mercy to the former and judgment to the latter.
The chapter begins with a vision of two baskets of figs, one good and one bad, used to symbolize God's treatment of different groups of people.
God promises to restore the exiles in Babylon and to bless them with a renewed relationship with Him.
God declares judgment on Zedekiah, his officials, and those who remained in Judah or fled to Egypt, calling them 'bad figs' unfit for salvation.
The chapter announces the coming destruction of Judah due to their disobedience and idolatry.
God's judgment is not limited to Judah but will extend to all surrounding nations and kings.

themes.theme: Inevitability of the Cup of Wrath
themes.what: The prophet is commanded to pour out the cup of divine wrath, which all nations must drink.
Rebellion against God leads to universal ruin, with no escape for any nation or ruler.
The chapter begins with Jeremiah being commanded by God to deliver a message of judgment to the people of Judah.
The people, including priests and prophets, react violently to Jeremiah's message, attempting to kill him.
Jeremiah asserts that he is speaking on behalf of the Lord and urges the people to repent.
The leaders of Judah are reminded of past prophets like Micah and Uriah, who were also persecuted for speaking truth.
Ahikam intervenes to protect Jeremiah from death, showing a moment of divine providence.
The chapter commands Judah and other nations to submit to the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, under threat of divine punishment.
The chapter warns against false prophets who claim the people will not serve Babylon and promises destruction for those who heed them.
The chapter asserts the LORD's authority over all nations and the certainty of His judgment and promises.
The chapter addresses the remaining temple vessels, stating they will remain in Babylon until the LORD brings them back.
A prophet claims that the yoke of Babylon will soon be broken, contradicting Jeremiah's message of continued subjugation.
God instructs Jeremiah to confront the false prophet and declare the true consequences of his lies.
The false prophet is judged by death, demonstrating the seriousness of false prophecy.
The chapter distinguishes between true and false prophets based on the outcome of their prophecies.
The chapter addresses the Israelites exiled in Babylon, urging them to settle and pray for the city’s peace.
The chapter warns the exiles against false prophets and diviners who claim to speak in God’s name but do not.
God promises to restore the exiles after seventy years and to bring them back to their homeland.
God threatens judgment on those who ignored His prophets and remained in Jerusalem.
God condemns Shemaiah for sending misleading letters to the exiles and priests.
The chapter announces the future return of the exiled Israelites and Judahites to their homeland.
God expresses anger over the people's sins and the suffering they have caused themselves.
God promises to heal the people and bring them relief from their suffering.
God promises to raise up a righteous leader and renew the covenant with the people.
The chapter warns of an imminent time of great distress and upheaval.
The chapter outlines God's promise to restore Israel and Judah, including a new covenant written on their hearts.
God promises to comfort the exiled people, bring them back to their land, and end their mourning.
The chapter declares that each person will be responsible for their own sins, not for the sins of their ancestors.
themes.words: עֲוֺן (sin), בֹּסֶר (sour grapes), תִּקְהֶינָה (teeth set on edge)

themes.what: God affirms the permanence of His promises and His sovereign control over creation and history.
themes.words: יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (LORD of Hosts), חֻקֹּת (ordinances), נְשָׂאָה (cease)

themes.what: God promises to rebuild Jerusalem and its surrounding areas, making them sacred and lasting.
God asserts His control over the fate of Jerusalem and its people, despite their rebellion.

themes.theme: Purchase of a field as a sign
themes.what: Jeremiah buys a field in Anathoth as a symbolic act of God's future restoration of the land.
The people are condemned for their idolatry and failure to follow God's laws.
God promises to restore His people to the land and make a new covenant with them.
God is portrayed as all-powerful, faithful, and just, with a deep knowledge of human actions.
The chapter emphasizes God's promise to restore Judah and Israel after their captivity and to bring peace and healing to the land.
It describes a future time when the land will be filled with joy, peace, and the sounds of celebration, indicating a return to divine favor.

themes.theme: Divine Covenant with David and Levi
themes.what: God reaffirms His covenant with David and the Levitical priests, ensuring their continued role in His plan.
The chapter uses the constancy of day and night to affirm the unbreakable nature of God's promises and covenants.
God refutes the people's belief that He has rejected them, asserting His ongoing commitment to His people.
God announces the destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonian king and Zedekiah's capture.
The people break a covenant to free Hebrew slaves, leading to divine condemnation.
God warns of severe punishment for breaking the covenant and ignoring His commands.
God recalls the covenant with the ancestors and emphasizes the seriousness of oaths.

themes.theme: The Rechabites' Obedience to Their Ancestor's Command
themes.what: The chapter recounts how the descendants of Jonadab the son of Rechab have faithfully followed his command not to drink wine or build houses, in contrast to the people of Judah.
God contrasts the Rechabites' obedience with the people of Judah's failure to heed His repeated commands and warnings through the prophets.
Because the people of Judah have not listened to God, He declares that He will bring upon them the evil He has spoken about.
God promises that the descendants of Jonadab will never be cut off, as a reward for their obedience to their ancestor's command.

themes.theme: Prophetic warning recorded in a scroll
themes.what: The chapter describes Jeremiah instructing Baruch to write down the Lord's messages about Judah's impending judgment and have them read publicly.
The people and officials hear the message and are afraid, but do not repent or take immediate action.

themes.theme: The king's rejection and destruction of the message
themes.what: King Jehoiakim burns the scroll after hearing part of it, showing his defiance and disregard for the Lord's word.
The Lord declares judgment on Jehoiakim for burning the scroll and rejecting the message, including the loss of his throne and death.

themes.theme: The message is preserved and continued
themes.what: Despite the destruction of the first scroll, Jeremiah instructs Baruch to write the message again, ensuring it is not lost.

themes.theme: Zedekiah's reign and rejection of prophecy
themes.what: The chapter begins by introducing King Zedekiah and his failure to heed the prophet Jeremiah's warnings.
Jeremiah is sent for by the king to pray, but is not imprisoned and continues to move freely among the people.
The arrival of Pharaoh's army causes the Chaldeans to withdraw, but Jeremiah warns that they will return and destroy Jerusalem.
Jeremiah is falsely accused of fleeing to the Chaldeans and is imprisoned by the officials.

themes.theme: Zedekiah's private inquiry and Jeremiah's plea
themes.what: The king secretly questions Jeremiah and is confronted with the truth of his own false prophets, while Jeremiah pleads not to be returned to prison.
Jeremiah is cast into a cistern by officials who see his message as harmful to the people's morale.
Ebed-Melech, a Cushite eunuch, intervenes to save Jeremiah from death by organizing his rescue.
Jeremiah warns Zedekiah that surrendering to Babylon will save his life, but the king is afraid and delays.
Jeremiah foretells the destruction of Jerusalem and the capture of Zedekiah if he refuses to surrender.
The officials do not act against Jeremiah despite his warning, as the word of the LORD remains unchallenged.
The chapter recounts the fall of Jerusalem to the Babylonians, including the capture of King Zedekiah and the destruction of the city.
It details the capture, judgment, and punishment of Zedekiah, including the death of his sons and his blinding.
The chapter describes the exile of the people of Judah to Babylon and the small number left in the land.
It records the special treatment of the prophet Jeremiah, who is spared and placed among the people.
The chapter concludes with a message from the Lord to Ebed-Melech, promising him salvation and protection.
Nebuzaradan releases Jeremiah from chains and gives him the choice to return to Babylon or remain in the land.
Gedaliah is appointed by Babylon to lead the remaining people in Judah, and others come to him for protection.
Leaders warn Gedaliah that Ismael is plotting to kill him, but he does not believe them.
Johanan suggests secretly killing Ismael to prevent disaster, but Gedaliah refuses.
The chapter recounts the murder of Gedaliah, the Babylonian-appointed governor of Judah, by Ishmael and his men.
Ishmael deceives a group of pilgrims traveling to Jerusalem and kills most of them, sparing only those who offer him material gain.
Ishmael flees to Ammon after the murder, but is pursued by Johanan and the survivors return to him.
The people fear the Babylonians due to Ishmael's actions and decide to flee to Egypt for safety.
The people ask Jeremiah to pray to God for guidance on whether to stay in the land or flee to Egypt.

themes.theme: God's warning against fleeing to Egypt
themes.what: God tells the people through Jeremiah that if they go to Egypt, they will face disaster, including death by sword, famine, and plague.
The people are rebuked for not listening to God's word and for deceiving themselves by making a false commitment to obey.

themes.theme: God's promise to those who remain faithful
themes.what: God promises to protect and restore those who remain in the land and obey His word.
The chapter opens with false leaders accusing Jeremiah of lying about God's command not to go to Egypt.
The leaders and people ignore God's command to remain in Judah and instead go to Egypt.
God commands Jeremiah to prophesy a coming judgment on Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar.
God warns the Jews in Egypt that their continued idolatry will bring destruction.
The people ignored God's prophets and persisted in their wickedness.
The people in Egypt reject Jeremiah's message and claim their idolatry brought prosperity.
God swears to bring judgment and declares that His word will stand.
God addresses Baruch, the scribe, through the prophet Jeremiah.
Baruch expresses his sorrow and lack of rest due to the burdens of the message he carries.
God declares that He will tear down and uproot what He has built and planted in the land.
God warns of coming calamity for all people and that Baruch's life will be at risk wherever he goes.
The chapter announces divine judgment against Egypt, particularly Pharaoh Neco, for his defeat and the coming invasion by Babylon.
The text describes Egypt's military forces as defeated and fleeing, with no hope of victory.
God is portrayed as sovereign, orchestrating events and taking vengeance on Egypt through Babylon.
Amid the judgment on Egypt, the chapter offers reassurance of God's protection and restoration for Israel.
The chapter announces an impending invasion and destruction of the Philistine cities by a northern power, as a judgment from the LORD.
The text describes the chaos and despair that will result from the invasion, with people crying out and collapsing from exhaustion.

themes.theme: Call to the sword to act
themes.what: The chapter personifies the sword as an instrument of the LORD, urging it to carry out the divine command against the Philistines.
The chapter announces and describes the destruction and shame of Moab by divine judgment.
Moab's leaders, cities, and people are to be disgraced and mocked for their pride and trust in false gods.
Moab's people and leaders will be taken into exile, and their cities will be abandoned and destroyed.
Moab's downfall is attributed to her pride and overconfidence in her strength and false security.
The chapter calls for mourning and wailing over the destruction of Moab and its people.
God declares coming destruction and exile for Ammon, followed by eventual restoration.
Edom is condemned for its pride and deceit, with its cities to be destroyed and its people scattered.

themes.theme: Judgment on Damascus and its allies
themes.what: Damascus and surrounding cities face destruction and silence from divine judgment.
Kedar and Hazor are to be plundered and abandoned by an invading force.
Elam is to be broken and scattered, with its rulers destroyed, though future restoration is promised.
The chapter announces the destruction of Babylon as judgment from God.
The chapter promises the return and restoration of Israel after Babylon's fall.
God's judgment is portrayed as inevitable and righteous, especially against Babylon.

themes.theme: Call to nations to attack Babylon
themes.what: The chapter calls on surrounding nations to rise up and destroy Babylon.

themes.theme: Babylon as a symbol of idolatry
themes.what: The chapter portrays Babylon as a place of idolatry and false worship.
The chapter announces the fall of Babylon through divine judgment and the actions of foreign invaders.
God's judgment is portrayed as righteous and necessary, especially in response to the suffering of Israel and Judah.
The people are urged to escape Babylon and to witness its downfall as a sign of God's power and judgment.
The chapter contrasts the false gods of Babylon with the true God of Israel, emphasizing the futility of idolatry.
The chapter concludes with instructions for delivering the message to Babylon and a symbolic act to confirm its fulfillment.
The chapter recounts the siege, capture, and destruction of Jerusalem by the Babylonians under Nebuchadrezzar and Nebuzaradan.
It details the deportation of the people of Judah to Babylon and the numbers of those taken in different years.
The chapter describes the capture, punishment, and imprisonment of King Zedekiah by the Babylonian king.

themes.theme: Destruction of the Temple and City
themes.what: It records the burning of the temple, royal palace, and the walls of Jerusalem by the Babylonians.
The chapter concludes with the release and favorable treatment of Jehoiachin, a former king of Judah, by the Babylonian king.
The chapter laments the fall of Jerusalem, describing her as a widow, abandoned by friends and comforters.
The chapter attributes Jerusalem's suffering to her sins and God's judgment for her rebellion.
The chapter describes the physical and social ruin of Jerusalem, including the capture of its people and leaders.
The chapter includes repeated appeals to God for comfort and intervention in the midst of suffering.
The chapter describes the devastation of Jerusalem and Judah as a result of God's anger and judgment.
The chapter details the physical and spiritual destruction of Jerusalem, including its palaces, strongholds, and religious institutions.
The chapter portrays the suffering of the people, especially the elderly, women, and children, during the siege and aftermath.
The chapter expresses deep sorrow and mourning for the loss of the city and its people, with calls for comfort and justice.
themes.words: עֵינַי חֳמַרְמְרוּ (my eyes have failed), נִשְׁפַּךְ (poured out), צָעַק (cried

themes.what: The chapter criticizes the false prophets who gave misleading visions and failed to warn the people of their sins.
The speaker describes intense physical and emotional suffering caused by divine judgment.
Amidst suffering, the speaker recalls and affirms the steadfast love and faithfulness of the LORD.
The speaker affirms that the LORD is just and does not act arbitrarily or without purpose.
The speaker calls for self-examination and a return to the LORD in repentance.
The speaker cries out to God for deliverance and affirms trust in His salvation.
The chapter laments the destruction and suffering of Jerusalem and its people, comparing their fate to historical catastrophes.
The text attributes the disaster to the people's sins, particularly the corruption of prophets and priests.
The chapter vividly describes the physical and emotional suffering of the people, especially children and the helpless.
The people are rejected by others and driven away, symbolizing their loss of identity and place.
The chapter portrays God's anger and judgment as the cause of the destruction and suffering.
The chapter laments the destruction and disgrace of Jerusalem and its people, describing their loss of land, freedom, and dignity.
The people acknowledge that their suffering is a result of the sins of their ancestors, which they now bear.
The chapter mourns the death or capture of leaders and the suffering of the young, symbolizing the collapse of the nation’s future.
The people express grief over the desolation of Mount Zion and the feeling that God has abandoned them.
The chapter ends with a prayer for God to return to His people and restore their former glory.
The chapter describes a vision Ezekiel receives of a divine being surrounded by celestial imagery, emphasizing God's majesty and power.
The vision includes four living creatures with multiple faces and wings, and wheels within wheels, symbolizing divine order and movement.
The chapter conveys the overwhelming presence and glory of God, causing Ezekiel to fall in reverence.
God commissions Ezekiel to speak to a rebellious people, despite their resistance.
The people of Israel are described as stubborn and rebellious, both in the present and historically.
Ezekiel is instructed to eat a scroll, symbolizing his acceptance of the message he must deliver.
Ezekiel is given a scroll to eat and is commissioned to speak to Israel despite their stubbornness.
Ezekiel is instructed to take God's words to heart and speak to the exiles, regardless of their response.
Ezekiel experiences a powerful vision of God's glory and is transported to the exiles.
Ezekiel is made a watchman to warn the people of Israel, with consequences for both the people and the prophet.
Ezekiel is bound and made mute, but will speak only when God commands.
The chapter describes a symbolic representation of the siege of Jerusalem through a model made of clay and an iron wall.
Ezekiel is commanded to lie on his side for 390 days and then 40 days to symbolically bear the guilt of Israel and Judah.
Ezekiel is instructed to eat and drink in a limited and symbolic manner to represent the hardship of the people in exile.
Ezekiel is told to bake his bread with dung to symbolize the humiliation and uncleanness of Israel in exile.
The chapter concludes with the declaration that the people will suffer due to their guilt and the breaking of the staff of bread and water.
The chapter begins with a symbolic act of cutting hair to represent the coming judgment on Jerusalem.
God accuses Jerusalem of despising His statutes and judgments and imitating the wickedness of surrounding nations.
The chapter describes the extreme consequences of God's judgment, including famine, plague, and cannibalism.
The judgment is to be carried out in the sight of the nations, making Jerusalem a disgrace and a warning.
God declares that He will not relent or show mercy, emphasizing the certainty of His spoken judgment.
The chapter announces YHWH's judgment against Israel through war, famine, and exile, targeting their religious practices and altars.
YHWH declares the destruction of altars, high places, and idols associated with Israel's worship.
The survivors will be scattered among the nations, but they will remember YHWH in exile.
The judgment is meant to make Israel and the nations recognize YHWH's authority and power.
The people will mourn their sins and idolatry in exile, acknowledging their wrongdoing.
The chapter repeatedly declares that the end and judgment have arrived for the land of Israel.
God expresses that He will not show mercy and will judge Israel according to their ways and their abominations.
The chapter describes the coming devastation, including war, famine, and death, with no hope for the people.
The people will seek peace and guidance but will find none, as their leaders and institutions fail.
Ezekiel is shown various forms of idolatry and abominations in the temple and Jerusalem.
God announces that He will act in fury and not show mercy due to the people's sins.
Ezekiel sees the elders of Israel secretly engaging in idolatrous practices.
Ezekiel witnesses women weeping for the idol Tammuz at the temple gate.
God authorizes the destruction of Jerusalem by marking the faithful and killing the rest.
A scribe-like figure is instructed to mark the foreheads of those who mourn the city's sins.
Six men are sent to kill indiscriminately, starting with the elders in the temple.
The prophet pleads for mercy, but God affirms the severity of the people's sins.
The chapter describes the glory of the Lord and its movement from the temple to the cherubim.
The cherubim are depicted in detail, including their appearance, wings, and movements.
The wheels associated with the cherubim are described, emphasizing their complexity and connection to the living creatures.
A man in linen is commanded to take fire from between the cherubim and scatter it over the city.
The chapter begins with the prophet being shown men in Jerusalem who are giving wicked advice and devising evil plans.
God declares that He knows the thoughts and intentions of the people of Israel, particularly their harmful actions.
Despite the judgment, God promises to gather the exiled Israelites and restore them to their land, giving them a new heart and spirit.
God announces that He will scatter the people among the nations and judge them for their disobedience and idolatry.
The chapter concludes with the departure of the glory of the LORD from Jerusalem to the mountain east of the city, symbolizing divine withdrawal.
Ezekiel is instructed to act out the coming exile to show the people of Israel their rebellion.
The people are described as rebellious, with eyes and ears but failing to see and hear the truth.
God declares that the visions and prophecies will be fulfilled soon, not delayed.
The land and its cities will be destroyed, and the people will be scattered among the nations.
God asserts His authority and presence through repeated declarations of 'I am the LORD'.
The chapter condemns false prophets who give deceptive visions and lies.
The prophets are compared to ineffective builders who fail to provide real protection for Israel.
Prophets are rebuked for falsely proclaiming peace when there is no peace.
The chapter extends its condemnation to women who prophesy falsely.
God declares judgment on the false prophets and promises to reveal His sovereignty.
The chapter condemns the elders of Israel for their idolatrous schemes and the false hope they seek from prophets.
God declares that He will bring judgment upon the land and its people for their sins, even if righteous individuals remain.
The chapter highlights that even righteous individuals like Noah, Daniel, and Job can only save themselves, not their families, in times of judgment.
The chapter explains that suffering serves to turn people away from sin and to demonstrate God's justice.
The chapter compares the vine tree to other trees, emphasizing its lack of practical value when burned.
The Lord declares that just as the vine tree is consumed by fire, so too will the people of Jerusalem be destroyed.
The chapter concludes with a declaration that the land will be made desolate due to the people's treachery.
God recounts Jerusalem's origins and condemns her for moral and spiritual unfaithfulness.
God describes His care for Jerusalem, including her spiritual and physical restoration.
Jerusalem is rebuked for idolatry, sacrificing children, and engaging in unfaithfulness to God.
God announces judgment for Jerusalem's sins, including destruction and shame.
Jerusalem is compared to Sodom and Samaria to highlight her greater sinfulness.

themes.theme: A Parable of Two Eagles and a Vine
themes.what: The chapter begins with a parable about two eagles and a vine, symbolizing the actions of kings and the fate of Judah.
It describes the king of Judah breaking a covenant with Babylon and seeking help from Egypt.
God declares judgment on the rebellious king and predicts his capture and death in Babylon.
The chapter ends with a promise from God to plant a new shoot from the cedar, symbolizing hope and restoration for Israel.
The chapter emphasizes that each person is responsible for their own actions and will be judged accordingly, not for the sins of their ancestors or descendants.
It describes what a righteous person does and how their righteousness leads to life, contrasting with the consequences of wickedness.
The chapter teaches that repentance can lead to redemption, even for the wicked, and that God desires people to turn from their sins and live.
The chapter addresses the fairness of God's judgment, asserting that God's ways are just and that people's own actions are the reason for their fate.
The chapter laments the downfall of Israel's rulers, comparing them to lions captured and silenced.
The chapter uses the metaphor of a vine to depict the former glory and subsequent destruction of Israel.
The chapter portrays the destruction of Israel as a result of divine anger and punishment.
The chapter recounts the Israelites' repeated disobedience to God's commandments and their idolatry in Egypt and the wilderness.
God emphasizes His covenant with Israel, His expectations, and the consequences of breaking it, including judgment and scattering.
God declares His holiness and the need for Israel to be sanctified through obedience and the keeping of His laws and Sabbaths.
God promises to gather the scattered Israelites, restore them to the land, and bring them to repentance and a renewed relationship with Him.

themes.theme: Divine Judgment by Fire and Sword
themes.what: The chapter announces a coming judgment from the Lord, described through fire and sword, to consume the land of Israel and its enemies.

themes.theme: Prophecy to the Negev and Jerusalem
themes.what: Ezekiel is commanded to prophesy against the forest of the Negev and the holy places of Jerusalem, signaling divine wrath.

themes.theme: Confusion and Capture of the People
themes.what: The judgment will cause confusion, fear, and the capture of the people of Israel, especially their leaders.

themes.theme: The Sword as a Symbol of Divine Action
themes.what: The sword is repeatedly used as a symbol of the Lord's judgment, sharpened and directed against the wicked and the righteous alike.
The people's reliance on false signs and oaths is condemned, and the Lord declares that their capture is inevitable.
The chapter announces divine judgment against Jerusalem for its widespread bloodshed and moral corruption.
The people have violated sacred laws, oppressed the vulnerable, and desecrated holy things.
God expresses anger and declares punishment, including scattering the people and destroying their city.
The leaders, priests, and prophets have failed to uphold justice or truth, and no one stood to protect the people.

themes.theme: Metaphor of Melting in a Furnace
themes.what: The people are compared to a mixed alloy to be melted in a furnace, symbolizing their destruction and purification.

themes.theme: Judgment for idolatry and spiritual adultery
themes.what: The chapter uses the allegory of two sisters, Aholah (Samaria) and Aholibah (Jerusalem), to depict their idolatry and unfaithfulness to God, leading to divine judgment.

themes.theme: Moral and religious corruption through foreign influence
themes.what: The sisters are shown to have been seduced by foreign nations (Assyria, Egypt, and Babylon), symbolizing the corruption of Israel and Judah through idolatrous alliances.
God declares that He will bring enemies to destroy the unfaithful cities, mirroring the fate of Samaria and threatening the same for Jerusalem.

themes.theme: Public disgrace and removal of religious symbols
themes.what: The judgment includes public humiliation, the stripping of religious and cultural symbols, and the destruction of their sacred spaces.

themes.theme: Warning to other nations and future correction
themes.what: The chapter ends with a warning to other nations to avoid the same fate and a promise of eventual moral restoration.
The chapter uses a parable of a boiling pot to symbolize the coming destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon.
God declares His anger against Jerusalem for its uncleanness and failure to repent, and states He will not delay in executing judgment.
Ezekiel is commanded to mourn in silence for his wife's death as a sign of the coming desolation of Israel.

themes.theme: Call to reflection and recognition of God's authority
themes.what: The people are challenged to recognize the signs and understand that God is acting according to His will.
God pronounces judgment on the Ammonites for rejoicing over Israel's destruction and defiling the sanctuary.
God declares judgment on Moab for considering itself equal to Judah and for its pride.
God announces judgment on Edom for taking vengeance against Judah and for its hostility.
God declares judgment on the Philistines for their vengeance and desire to destroy Israel.
The chapter repeatedly emphasizes that God will execute His judgments and that the nations will know He is the LORD.
The chapter announces a complete and devastating judgment from the Lord against the city of Tyre for its arrogance and destruction of Jerusalem.
The Lord declares that Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, will lead a powerful military campaign against Tyre, destroying it completely.
The chapter describes the total ruin of Tyre, including the destruction of its walls, towers, and people, and its transformation into a place of desolation.
The rulers of the sea and surrounding islands will mourn the fall of Tyre, recognizing the power of the Lord.
The judgment culminates in Tyre being brought down to the dead and erased from the land of the living, never to be rebuilt.
themes.words: יָרְדוּ מֵעַל כִּסְאוֹתָם, לְמַעַן לֹא תֵשֵׁבִי, לֹא תִמָּצְאִי

themes.what: The chapter describes Tyre's wealth and its role as a central hub of international trade, listing the goods and peoples involved.
The chapter prophesies the downfall of Tyre, describing its destruction in the sea and the mourning of its trading partners.
The chapter includes a lament over Tyre, showing the grief of its people and the traders who relied on it.
The chapter highlights the global influence of Tyre, showing how its destruction affects many nations and their leaders.

themes.theme: Pride and downfall of the king of Tyre
themes.what: The chapter pronounces judgment on the king of Tyre for his pride and self-deification, declaring his destruction.

themes.theme: Divine judgment and the fall of a symbolic cherub
themes.what: The king of Tyre is compared to a fallen cherub in Eden, who was cast out for iniquity and pride.
The chapter extends divine judgment to the city of Sidon, threatening it with plague, bloodshed, and destruction.
The chapter concludes with a promise of Israel's restoration and the LORD's sanctification among them.
The chapter announces the downfall of Pharaoh and Egypt as divine punishment for their arrogance and failure to support Israel.
The prophecy declares that Egypt will become a wasteland for forty years, symbolizing its total destruction and abandonment.
After forty years of desolation, Egypt will be restored, but as a lowly and diminished kingdom.
The chapter states that Nebuchadrezzar will be given Egypt as a reward for his labor in serving the Lord.
The ultimate purpose of these events is to demonstrate the Lord's sovereignty and to bring recognition of His power.
The chapter announces the coming destruction and judgment of Egypt by the Lord, including the fall of its military and political strength.
The Lord declares His authority over the nations, showing that He will execute His judgment and be known through it.
The chapter identifies Nebuchadrezzar, king of Babylon, as the instrument through which the Lord will carry out His judgment on Egypt.

themes.theme: Destruction of Egyptian Idols and Power
themes.what: The Lord declares the end of Egypt's idolatry and the collapse of its religious and political symbols.
The Lord announces that the people of Egypt will be dispersed among the nations as part of His judgment.
The chapter uses the metaphor of a mighty cedar to describe Assyria's former glory and its downfall.
God announces judgment against Pharaoh and Egypt, comparing their pride to Assyria's and predicting their destruction.
The chapter describes how the natural world reacts to the downfall of the mighty cedar, with animals and plants being affected.
God expresses mourning for the fallen cedar and describes how other trees in the garden are comforted by its fall.
The chapter warns against pride, showing how the cedar's exaltation led to its downfall.
The chapter delivers a divine message of judgment against Pharaoh and Egypt, describing their downfall and destruction.
A lament is called for over Egypt's former strength and its people, emphasizing their fall into the grave.
Egypt is compared to other nations that have also fallen and been destroyed, reinforcing the inevitability of divine judgment.
The chapter outlines the role of a watchman who warns people of impending judgment and the consequences for both the watchman and the people.
God emphasizes that He does not desire the death of the wicked, but calls for repentance and offers life to those who turn from their sins.
The people accuse God of injustice, but He clarifies that their own actions are the cause of their suffering.
A fugitive confirms the fall of Jerusalem, and the chapter describes the divine judgment and desolation of the land.
The people pretend to listen to the prophet, but their hearts remain unchanged and they do not act on his words.
The chapter condemns the shepherds of Israel for neglecting and exploiting the flock.
God declares that He will personally care for His flock and replace the corrupt shepherds.
God promises to gather His scattered people and restore them to their land.
God will judge the corrupt shepherds and those who oppress the weak.
God promises a future covenant of peace and prosperity for His people.
God announces a judgment of destruction and desolation on Mount Seir for its hostility toward Israel.
The judgment is explained as a response to the hatred and envy of Edom toward Israel, especially during Israel's downfall.
God declares that He has heard the taunts and boasts of Edom and will respond in kind.
The chapter concludes with a direct comparison between Edom's joy at Israel's ruin and the desolation that will come upon Edom itself.
God promises to restore the land of Israel and its people after their exile and desolation.
God explains that Israel was scattered because they defiled the land with their idolatry and wickedness.

themes.theme: Cleansing and Renewal of the People
themes.what: God promises to cleanse the people, give them a new heart and spirit, and make them His people again.
The desolate cities and land will be rebuilt and made fruitful, showing God's power and faithfulness.
God's actions are for the sake of His holy name and to demonstrate His greatness to the nations.
God shows the prophet a vision of dry bones coming back to life, symbolizing the restoration of Israel.
God promises to gather the dispersed people of Israel and return them to their land.
God unites the divided tribes of Israel under one leadership and one covenant.
God promises an eternal covenant of peace with Israel, including His presence among them.
The chapter begins with a divine command for the prophet to prophesy against Gog, a leader of a coalition of nations.
The chapter describes Gog's future invasion of Israel, including the gathering of a large and well-equipped army.
God declares that He will judge Gog and his forces with divine wrath and natural disasters.
The chapter concludes with the purpose of the judgment: to demonstrate God's power and sanctify His name before many nations.
The chapter describes the coming defeat of Gog, a foreign leader, and his army by divine intervention.
The chapter outlines the process of purifying the land of Israel after the battle, including the burial of the dead and the burning of weapons.
The chapter emphasizes the display of God's glory and judgment to the nations through the defeat of Gog and the subsequent events.
The chapter concludes with a promise of the restoration of Israel and the reestablishment of God's covenant with them.
The chapter describes a vision of a temple complex, including its gates, walls, measurements, and surrounding structures.
The text provides precise measurements for the temple's gates, walls, courtyards, and other architectural features.
The chapter specifies roles for priests, particularly the sons of Zadok, in maintaining the temple and its rituals.
The chapter provides detailed measurements of the temple's various parts, including the porch, inner courtyard, and the Holy of Holies.
It describes the architectural features of the temple, including side panels, doors, and decorative elements like cherubim and palm trees.
The chapter specifies the interior and exterior details of the temple, including the placement of windows, carvings, and the structure of the altar.
The chapter details the measurements and layout of chambers in the temple complex, particularly those in the outer courtyard.
It identifies specific chambers as holy places where priests eat and store sacred offerings.
The chapter concludes with a detailed measurement of the entire temple complex, emphasizing its square and enclosed form.

themes.theme: The Glory of God Enters the Temple
themes.what: The chapter describes the vision of the glory of the Lord entering the temple through the eastern gate and filling the house.

themes.theme: God's Presence and Dwelling Among Israel
themes.what: God declares the temple as the place of His throne and His feet, where He will dwell among Israel forever, provided they no longer defile His name.

themes.theme: Instructions for the Temple and Its Measurements
themes.what: The chapter provides detailed measurements and instructions for the temple, its altar, and surrounding areas.

themes.theme: Atonement and Purification of the Temple
themes.what: The chapter outlines the process of atonement for the altar and temple through sacrifices, including sin offerings and burnt offerings.
The Lord declares that the eastern gate of the temple will remain permanently closed because He has entered through it.

themes.theme: The Glory of the Lord in the Temple
themes.what: The prophet is shown the glory of the Lord filling the temple, causing him to fall on his face in reverence.
The Lord rebukes Israel for bringing foreign and uncircumcised people into the sanctuary and for breaking the covenant.

themes.theme: Role of the Levites and Priests
themes.what: The Levites are assigned roles in the temple, while the priests of Zadok are given specific duties and privileges.
Detailed rules are given for the priests' clothing, conduct, marriage, and purity, emphasizing holiness and separation.
The chapter outlines the apportioning of land in Israel, including a holy portion for the sanctuary and specific areas for priests and Levites.
It addresses the leaders of Israel, calling them to cease oppression and to act justly and righteously toward the people.
The chapter specifies standard measures for weights, bushels, and shekels, along with required tributes and offerings from the people.
It describes the sacrificial duties of the prince and priests, especially for purification of the sanctuary and atonement for the people.
Describes the specific offerings the prince must make on the Sabbath and new moon, including the number and type of animals and the accompanying grain and oil offerings.

themes.theme: Regulations for the Prince's Access to the Temple
themes.what: Outlines the procedures for the prince entering and exiting the temple, including the specific gate he must use and the rituals performed upon his arrival.
Specifies the daily burnt offering that must be made to the Lord, including the lamb, grain offering, and oil, to be performed every morning without fail.
Lays out the rules regarding the prince's inheritance, ensuring that land given to his sons remains with them, while land given to servants is returned after the year of release.
Describes the location and purpose of the temple kitchens where priests and servants prepare sacrifices, ensuring sanctification of the people.
The chapter describes a vision of water flowing from the temple, increasing in depth and bringing life to the land and its creatures.

themes.theme: Healing and restoration of the Dead Sea
themes.what: The river flows into the Dead Sea, transforming it from a salty, lifeless body of water into one that supports life and healing.
Trees growing along the river's banks are described as bearing fruit continuously and never losing their leaves.
God outlines the boundaries of the land to be divided among the twelve tribes of Israel, including provisions for foreigners.

themes.theme: Inclusion of foreigners in the inheritance
themes.what: God commands that foreigners who live among the Israelites and have children with them should be included in the land inheritance.
The chapter outlines the allocation of land to each of the twelve tribes of Israel in the promised land.
A portion of the land is set apart as a sacred offering for the sanctuary and the priests.
The Levites and the priests receive specific portions of land adjacent to the holy offering.
A city is described with its surrounding buffer zone, and its gates are named after the tribes.
A section of land is designated for the ruler, adjacent to the holy offering and the city.
The chapter begins with the Babylonian invasion of Jerusalem and the capture of King Jehoiakim and sacred objects from the temple.
The Babylonian king orders the selection of Israelite youths for training in Babylonian culture and language.
Daniel refuses to eat the king's food and wine, choosing instead a simpler diet, and convinces the steward to test it.
God grants Daniel and his companions wisdom and understanding, surpassing the king's advisors.
Daniel and his companions are presented to the king and excel in service, standing before him in favor.

themes.theme: Divine revelation of a king's dream
themes.what: The chapter recounts how Daniel receives a vision from God revealing the meaning of King Nebuchadnezzar's dream about a statue representing future kingdoms.

themes.theme: The threat to the wise men of Babylon
themes.what: The king threatens to execute all the wise men of Babylon if they cannot reveal the dream and its meaning, prompting Daniel to intervene.

themes.theme: Daniel's faith and prayer to God
themes.what: Daniel seeks God's help to reveal the mystery, and God answers him in a vision during the night.

themes.theme: The vision of the great statue and its interpretation
themes.what: Daniel describes a vision of a statue made of different materials, which symbolizes successive kingdoms, and explains its meaning to the king.
The king honors Daniel for his wisdom and faithfulness, granting him high status and authority in Babylon.
The chapter describes Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego's refusal to bow to a golden image set up by King Nebuchadnezzar.
The three men are thrown into a furnace, but they are miraculously unharmed, and a fourth figure is seen with them.
Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges the power of the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and issues a decree in His honor.
The chapter concludes with the king promoting the three men for their faithfulness and issuing a proclamation of peace.
The chapter describes the downfall of King Nebuchadnezzar as a result of his pride and his eventual restoration after humbling himself before God.

themes.theme: The vision of the great tree
themes.what: Nebuchadnezzar has a vision of a great tree representing his kingdom, which is destroyed by divine decree but left with a stump to symbolize the continuation of his rule in a humbled state.
Daniel, known as Belteshazzar, is called upon to interpret the king's dream, showing his wisdom and the presence of divine spirit in him.

themes.theme: The sovereignty of God over kingdoms
themes.what: The chapter emphasizes that the Most High God rules over the kingdoms of the world and can raise or humble whomever He chooses.
After being humbled and living like a beast for seven years, Nebuchadnezzar is restored to his kingdom and acknowledges God's power.
The chapter recounts how Belshazzar's arrogant actions provoke divine judgment, symbolized by a mysterious hand writing a prophetic message on the wall.
Belshazzar and his court are condemned for praising false gods made of lifeless materials, contrasting with the living God.
Daniel is summoned to interpret the divine message, revealing his unique wisdom and role in the kingdom.
The chapter concludes with the immediate downfall of Belshazzar and the transfer of power to the Medes and Persians.
The chapter highlights Daniel's unwavering faithfulness and trustworthiness in the face of political opposition.
The administrators and satraps conspire to trap Daniel by exploiting the king's new decree.
God intervenes to protect Daniel from the lions, demonstrating His power and faithfulness.
The conspirators who falsely accused Daniel are punished by being thrown into the lions' den.
The king publicly acknowledges the living God and His eternal dominion.
Daniel describes a vision of four great beasts rising from the sea, each representing a future kingdom.

themes.theme: The Ancient of Days and Judgment
themes.what: Daniel sees the Ancient of Days seated in judgment, with books opened and a stream of fire flowing from him.

themes.theme: The Son of Man Receiving Dominion
themes.what: A figure like a son of man is given eternal dominion and glory by the Ancient of Days.
An angel explains the meaning of the vision, identifying the beasts as future kingdoms and the final judgment.
Daniel is troubled by the vision and reflects on its meaning, showing the emotional impact of the prophecy.

themes.theme: A Vision of Ram and Goat
themes.what: The chapter describes a vision of a ram and a goat, which symbolize different kingdoms.
Gabriel explains the vision to Daniel, identifying the symbols and their meanings.
The vision foretells the rise and fall of future kingdoms, including Greece and its successors.
The vision includes a prophecy about a time of desolation and the eventual cleansing of the sanctuary.
The speaker confesses the sins of Israel and acknowledges God's righteousness.
The chapter emphasizes that God's judgment is just and has been fulfilled through the destruction of Jerusalem.
Gabriel reveals a prophecy about seventy weeks of years for the people and the holy city.
The speaker pleads for God to have mercy on Jerusalem and His people.

themes.theme: A Vision of a Heavenly Being
themes.what: Daniel sees a vision of a powerful, divine figure who speaks to him and explains the vision.
There is a spiritual battle between the ruler of Persia and the angel Michael, with the ruler of Greece soon to arrive.
Daniel mourns and fasts for three weeks, showing his devotion to God.
The heavenly being reassures Daniel and strengthens him to understand the vision.
The vision is about future events that will affect Daniel's people at the end of days.
The chapter outlines a sequence of future kings, particularly focusing on the rise and fall of the kings of the North and South, and their ongoing conflicts.
It describes the desecration of the holy place and the breaking of covenants, particularly through the actions of a future king who opposes the holy covenant.
The chapter mentions the endurance and wisdom of those who know their God, contrasting them with those who fall away or are destroyed.

themes.theme: The end-time ruler and his arrogance
themes.what: It prophesies the rise of a powerful and arrogant ruler who will exalt himself above all gods and bring destruction.
The chapter concludes with a prophecy of a final invasion, destruction, and the ruler's ultimate downfall.
The chapter describes a time of great distress and the eventual salvation of God's people.
It speaks of a resurrection of the dead, with some receiving eternal life and others eternal disgrace.
The wise will shine and be rewarded, while the wicked will be tested and ultimately condemned.
The visions are to remain hidden until the time of the end, when they will be understood.
Specific time periods are given for the duration of suffering and the ultimate end of evil.

themes.what: God announces punishment for Israel's unfaithfulness through the prophet Hosea.
Hosea's marriage to a prostitute and their children symbolize Israel's covenant unfaithfulness.

themes.what: God distinguishes between Israel and Judah, showing mercy to the latter but not the former.
The chapter describes God's judgment on Israel for their unfaithfulness, followed by a promise of future restoration and reconciliation.
Israel is portrayed as an unfaithful wife who turns to other lovers and uses divine gifts for idolatry.
God promises a new covenant with Israel, including peace with nature and the removal of war.
God renews Israel's identity as His people and promises a restored relationship marked by faithfulness and mercy.
The chapter presents God's enduring love for Israel despite their unfaithfulness, using the metaphor of a marriage.
The prophet symbolically redeems an unfaithful woman, representing God's redemptive action toward Israel.
The chapter foretells a time when Israel will return to God and seek His guidance and leadership.
The chapter describes the widespread corruption and idolatry in Israel, including lying, murder, adultery, and forsaking God.
God announces judgment on the people and the land for their sins, including destruction and dishonor.

themes.theme: Rejection of knowledge and divine teaching
themes.what: The people are condemned for their ignorance of God and His teachings, leading to their downfall.
The people turn to false gods and idols, offering sacrifices to them instead of to the true God.
Both the people and their leaders (including priests) are held accountable for their sins and will suffer together.
The chapter announces God's judgment against the priests, the house of Israel, and the house of the king for their spiritual unfaithfulness and idolatry.
The people, especially Ephraim and Israel, are condemned for spiritual unfaithfulness, like adultery, and for not knowing the Lord.
The people's religious rituals and sacrifices are shown to be ineffective because they are not accompanied by true repentance or faith.
God declares that He has turned away from the people, but also asserts His presence and power in judgment and faithfulness.
The chapter begins with an invitation to return to the LORD, emphasizing His power to heal and restore.
The people are criticized for their lack of true knowledge of God, despite their religious rituals.
The people are accused of breaking their covenant with God through betrayal and idolatry.
God expresses frustration and announces judgment against the people and their leaders.
themes.words: חָצַבְתִּי (torn), זִמָּה (conspiracy), שָׁת קָצִיר (reap the harvest)

themes.what: The chapter pronounces judgment on Israel for their deceit, idolatry, and moral corruption.
Israel's rejection of God is described, along with the resulting divine punishment and exile.
God asserts His control over Israel's fate, using metaphors of fire and nets to depict His judgment.
The people's misplaced trust in foreign powers and their eventual humiliation are highlighted.
The chapter laments Israel's violation of the covenant and rejection of God's teaching.
It describes Israel's creation and worship of idols, particularly the golden calf in Samaria.
The chapter outlines the judgment and suffering that will come upon Israel due to their sins.
It critiques Israel's misguided leadership and futile religious practices.
The chapter emphasizes that God will not forget their sins and will bring judgment upon them.

themes.theme: Divine Judgment for Idolatry and Infidelity
themes.what: The chapter pronounces judgment on Israel for abandoning God and pursuing false gods and materialism.

themes.theme: Loss of Blessings and Sacred Practices
themes.what: Israel will lose its religious and agricultural blessings, including the ability to offer sacrifices and partake in festivals.
The people repeat past sins, such as those at Baal-peor, showing a pattern of disobedience and idolatry.
Israel will be driven from the land and dispersed among the nations, with their leaders and children perishing.

themes.theme: Fertility Cursed and Lineage Cut Off
themes.what: God will curse Israel's fertility, ensuring their lineage is not sustained through future generations.
The chapter describes God's judgment on Israel for their idolatry and covenant violations, including the destruction of their religious symbols and the loss of their leadership.
The people are depicted as having abandoned true worship, made false covenants, and engaged in unjust and deceptive practices.
God calls Israel to return to Him through righteous living and to seek Him while there is still time.

themes.theme: God's love and care for Israel
themes.what: The chapter begins by emphasizing God's deep love and care for Israel, especially Ephraim, whom He raised and protected.
The chapter highlights Israel's unfaithfulness, as they turned away from God to worship false gods like Baals and idols.
The chapter describes the coming judgment and suffering that Israel will face as a result of their rebellion, including exile and war.
Despite Israel's failures, God expresses His compassion and restraint, stating He will not destroy them completely because He is holy and not a man.
The chapter concludes with a message of hope, as God promises to restore Israel and lead them back to their homes.
The chapter condemns Israel and Ephraim for their deceit, greed, and idolatry, highlighting their moral and spiritual failures.
God recalls His covenant with Jacob and Israel, emphasizing His role as their redeemer and the need for repentance.
The chapter references Israel's history, including Jacob's struggles and the role of prophets in Israel's journey.
The chapter calls Israel to return to God through acts of love, justice, and faithful waiting.
The chapter condemns Israel for turning to false gods and making idols, which leads to their downfall.
God asserts that He alone is the true and saving God, and that there is no other.
Israel is punished for forgetting God after being sustained by Him in the wilderness.
God declares that He will bring judgment upon Israel, using metaphors of wild animals and natural forces.
Despite judgment, there is a brief mention of God's power to redeem from death and Sheol.
The chapter begins with a call for Israel to return to God after having sinned and rebelled against Him.
God promises to heal and restore Israel, comparing His care to dew and the flourishing of a lily and olive tree.
The chapter rejects reliance on Assyria and human-made idols, affirming trust in God alone.
The chapter concludes by urging understanding of God's righteous ways and the fate of the wicked.

themes.theme: A Call to Lament Over a Devastating Locust Plague
themes.what: The chapter describes a severe locust plague that has destroyed the land's crops and resources, prompting a call for mourning and reflection.

themes.theme: A Call to Religious Repentance and Fasting
themes.what: The prophet urges the people, especially the priests and elders, to respond to the disaster with repentance, fasting, and a solemn assembly before God.

themes.theme: The Nearness of the Day of the LORD
themes.what: The devastation is linked to a coming judgment, with the 'day of the LORD' described as a time of destruction and divine reckoning.
The prophet calls for the story of the plague to be passed down through generations as a lesson and reminder.

themes.theme: Divine Judgment and the Day of the Lord
themes.what: The chapter begins with a vivid description of the Day of the Lord as a time of divine judgment, using imagery of a powerful invading army and natural disasters.
The chapter shifts to a call for the people to repent through fasting, weeping, and mourning, emphasizing heartfelt change over outward displays.
The people are called to gather in a solemn assembly, including all members of society, to participate in a communal act of repentance and worship.
God promises to show mercy, restore abundance, and deliver the people from their enemies, reversing the devastation and bringing blessings.
Declares that God's Spirit will be poured out on all people, including future generations and servants.
Announces signs such as blood, fire, and darkness as precursors to a great day of the LORD.
States that those who call on the name of the LORD will be rescued, especially in Jerusalem.
God announces a future judgment against the nations who have oppressed Israel, gathering them in the Valley of Jehoshaphat for divine reckoning.
God promises to restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem and to bring peace and prosperity to the land.
A call is issued to the nations to prepare for war, symbolizing the coming of divine judgment and the need for readiness.
God condemns the nations, including Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistines, for their exploitation and mistreatment of Israel.
God affirms His dwelling in Zion and His sovereignty over Israel and the nations, emphasizing His role as judge and protector.
The chapter announces divine judgment against Damascus for its violent oppression of Gilead's women.
The chapter declares punishment for Gaza's involvement in the forced deportation and sale of people to Edom.
The chapter pronounces judgment on Tyre for its betrayal of brotherly covenant and deportation of people to Edom.
The chapter condemns Edom for their violent and vengeful treatment of their brother Israelites.
The chapter announces divine retribution against Ammon for their brutal act of killing pregnant women in Gilead.
The chapter announces divine judgment against Moab for burning the bones of the Edomite king.
The chapter pronounces judgment on Judah for despising God's law and following ancestral idolatry.
The chapter declares judgment on Israel for selling the righteous, oppressing the poor, and profaning God's name.
The chapter recalls God's faithfulness in delivering Israel from Egypt and destroying the Amorites.
The chapter accuses Israel of silencing prophets and corrupting religious practice.
God declares that He holds Israel accountable for their sins because He chose them.
The chapter uses rhetorical questions to show that divine action is inevitable and purposeful.
God reveals His plans to the prophets before acting.

themes.theme: Call to witness Israel's sin and coming judgment
themes.what: The surrounding nations are called to witness the coming judgment on Samaria.

themes.theme: Destruction of religious and elite structures
themes.what: God threatens to destroy the altars and luxurious homes of the people.
The chapter condemns the rich women of Samaria for exploiting the poor and promises divine punishment.
God recounts a series of calamities He has sent to Israel, none of which caused them to repent.
The chapter ends with a final warning and call for Israel to prepare to meet their God.
The chapter concludes by affirming God's power as the creator of all things.
The chapter announces the fall and destruction of Israel due to their sins.
The people are urged to seek the Lord and live, rather than relying on religious rituals.
The Lord rejects Israel's festivals and sacrifices because they are not accompanied by justice and righteousness.
The chapter condemns the oppression of the poor and the perversion of justice in the courts.

themes.theme: The Day of the Lord as Judgment
themes.what: The anticipated 'day of the Lord' is described as a day of darkness and destruction, not salvation.
The chapter denounces the people of Israel for their arrogance, comfort, and moral decay.
It announces that God will bring severe punishment and exile upon them for their sins.
The chapter criticizes the people for distorting justice and righteousness.
It foretells that a foreign nation will rise against Israel and subdue them.
The chapter presents three visions of judgment—locusts, fire, and a plumb line—that God shows the prophet Amos to warn Israel of coming destruction.
Amos intercedes with God to spare Israel, and God relents twice, showing a pattern of mercy before judgment.
Amos faces opposition from a priest who tries to silence him, but Amos asserts his divine calling and warns of further judgment.
The chapter ends with a detailed prophecy of Israel's destruction, including the fall of its religious institutions and the exile of its people.
The chapter announces divine judgment against Israel for exploiting the poor and corrupting justice.
God declares He will no longer show mercy to Israel and that their time is up.
The chapter describes the coming devastation, including the collapse of religious and social life.
A future famine is predicted, not of food or water, but of the word of the Lord.
The chapter condemns those who make false oaths and place trust in false religious symbols.
The chapter begins with a vivid vision of God's judgment upon Israel, emphasizing the inevitability and completeness of destruction for the guilty.
God declares that no place is beyond His reach, whether in Sheol, heaven, or the sea, reinforcing His omnipotence in carrying out judgment.
The chapter affirms God's control over natural forces, such as the earth, rivers, and the heavens, as part of His authority.
Despite judgment, the chapter ends with a promise of future restoration, including the rebuilding of Israel and its prosperity.
God declares that He will not completely destroy Israel, distinguishing them from other nations and showing partial mercy.
The chapter announces the judgment and destruction of Edom for its arrogance and failure to show mercy to Israel.
God declares that the nations will face the same fate as Edom for their actions, emphasizing retribution and fairness.
The chapter concludes with a vision of Israel's future restoration and the holy presence of God on Mount Zion.
God commands Jonah to go to Nineveh and proclaim its wickedness.
Jonah flees from God's command to Tarshish, boarding a ship.
A great storm is sent by God, threatening to destroy the ship.
Jonah sleeps while the sailors panic and pray to their gods.
Jonah reveals his identity and offers himself to be thrown into the sea.
Jonah prays to God from the belly of the fish, recounting his distress and God's deliverance.
Jonah describes being rescued from the depths of the sea and brought back to life.
Jonah resolves to offer a thanksgiving sacrifice to God for his salvation.
God gives Jonah a second command to go to Nineveh and proclaim a message.
Jonah follows God's command and begins to proclaim the message in the city.
The people of Nineveh, including the king, respond with fasting, sackcloth, and repentance.
God sees their repentance and decides not to carry out the destruction he had threatened.
Jonah expresses intense anger and wishes for death because God did not destroy Nineveh as he expected.
God challenges Jonah's anger twice, asking if it is justified.
God uses the growth and withering of a gourd to teach Jonah about compassion and concern.
God concludes the chapter by affirming His concern for the people and animals of Nineveh.

themes.theme: Divine Judgment on Israel and Judah
themes.what: The chapter announces God's coming judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem for their sins.
The chapter describes the physical destruction of cities and the destruction of idols and religious symbols.
The prophet expresses deep sorrow and mourning over the coming disaster.

themes.theme: Call to Repentance and Warning to Neighboring Cities
themes.what: The chapter warns not only Israel and Judah but also neighboring cities to not rejoice or be complacent.
The chapter denounces those who plot iniquity and oppress others, warning of divine judgment.
God announces a time of punishment and a lament for the people who have been plundered and ruined.
The chapter affirms that God's words are upright and His path is just, countering false claims about His anger.
God promises to gather the remnant of Israel and protect them under His care.
The chapter condemns the leaders of Israel for their corruption and failure to uphold justice.
The chapter denounces false prophets who mislead the people and prepare them for disaster.
The chapter announces the coming judgment on Jerusalem and Zion due to the people's sins.
The chapter envisions a future where nations come to the mountain of the LORD to learn His ways and walk in His paths.
It describes a time of peace where weapons are transformed into tools for agriculture and war is no longer learned.
God promises to gather the broken and scattered people of Israel and make them strong under His reign.
The chapter laments the suffering of Jerusalem, comparing it to a woman in labor, and predicts her exile to Babylon.
The nations that gather against Jerusalem do not understand God's purpose, which is to gather them for judgment.
The chapter announces the birth of a future ruler of Israel who will come from Bethlehem and have ancient origins.
The chapter describes a future time when peace will come, even in the face of Assyrian invasion, through divine shepherds and rulers.
The chapter speaks of the remnant of Jacob being strong and flourishing among the nations, like a lion and dew from the Lord.
The chapter includes a series of divine judgments against the people, including the destruction of military and idolatrous elements.
God calls the mountains and earth to witness his lawsuit against his people for their disobedience and ingratitude.

themes.what: The chapter laments the moral decay of society and the destruction that follows the wickedness of leaders and people.
The speaker expresses trust in God as the only source of salvation and light in a time of darkness.
The chapter looks forward to a time when God will restore His people and show them mercy.
The chapter praises God for being unlike other gods and for His willingness to forgive and show steadfast love.
The chapter emphasizes God's anger, vengeance, and unstoppable power against Nineveh.
The chapter describes the inevitable destruction and desolation that will come to Nineveh.
Amidst the judgment, the chapter affirms God's goodness and protection for those who trust in Him.
The chapter condemns Nineveh for its wickedness and plotting against God.
The chapter announces the downfall and destruction of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital.
The chapter describes the chaos and collapse of Nineveh's military and defenses.
The chapter portrays the humiliation and loss of status of Nineveh's leaders and people.
The chapter emphasizes that the Lord is the one who brings about the destruction.
The chapter announces and describes the destruction and disgrace of Nineveh as a city of violence and seduction.
Nineveh is condemned for its bloodshed, deceit, and exploitation of nations.
The city faces imminent and overwhelming military destruction, with its defenses failing.
Nineveh will be exposed and disgraced before nations and kingdoms.
Nineveh is compared to No-Amon, a city that also fell despite its defenses.
The prophet Habakkuk laments to God about the prevalence of violence and the failure of justice.
God announces that He will raise up the Chaldeans as an instrument of judgment upon the people.

themes.theme: Reflection on divine justice and sovereignty
themes.what: The prophet questions God's silence and reflects on His holiness and role as the just judge.
The chapter describes the ruthless behavior of the Chaldeans and their exploitation of others.
The prophet compares humanity to fish without a ruler, emphasizing human helplessness.
God instructs the prophet to write a vision that will come to pass in due time, emphasizing the certainty of its fulfillment despite seeming delay.
A series of 'woe' oracles condemn the wicked for their greed, violence, and idolatry, with divine judgment promised.

themes.theme: God's glory will fill the earth
themes.what: The chapter concludes with a declaration that the knowledge of the Lord's glory will cover the earth like water over the sea.
The futility of idolatry is highlighted, showing that idols are lifeless and cannot save or speak.
The chapter ends with a call for all the earth to be silent before the Lord in his holy temple.
Describes the awe-inspiring arrival and power of God, emphasizing His glory and control over nature and nations.
Portrays God's destructive power as He judges the wicked and subdues nations through fire, plague, and force.
Reflects on the speaker's fear and the world's distress, followed by a declaration of trust in God despite hardship.
Illustrates the impact of God's actions on the natural world, including mountains, rivers, and celestial bodies.
Concludes with the speaker's resolve to trust in God's salvation and strength despite the surrounding chaos.
The chapter announces a sweeping divine judgment on the earth and especially on Judah for their sins.
It lists specific sins, including idolatry, false worship, and complacency toward God.
God is described as watching and waiting for the time to act against the complacent and wicked.
The chapter predicts the downfall of rulers, the wealthy, and those who exploit others.
It declares that silver and gold cannot save people on the day of the Lord’s wrath.
The chapter warns of the coming wrath of the LORD and the destruction of several nations and cities as punishment for their sins.
The chapter calls the humble and righteous to seek the LORD and righteousness in anticipation of the coming judgment.

themes.theme: Destruction of Philistia and Philistine cities
themes.what: The chapter specifically prophesies the abandonment and ruin of Philistine cities like Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron.
The chapter extends the prophecy of judgment to Moab, Ammon, Cush, and Assyria for their hostility toward Israel.
The chapter concludes with a vision of the remnant of Judah inheriting the land once occupied by the Philistines.
The chapter pronounces judgment on Jerusalem for her rebellion and failure to trust in God.
God is described as just and will not allow iniquity to go unpunished.
The chapter promises future restoration, salvation, and a renewed relationship with God for the faithful remnant.
God will bring all nations to worship Him with a unified purpose.
The people are rebuked for not rebuilding the house of the LORD while living in comfort.
The people are urged to consider their ways and the consequences of their neglect.
The LORD explains that the people's lack of prosperity is due to His judgment on the land.
The leaders and people respond to the message and begin to rebuild the temple.
The chapter addresses the people's discouragement over the temple's humble state compared to its former glory and encourages them to continue the work.
God reassures the people of His presence with them and reminds them of the covenant made with their ancestors.
God promises a future where the temple will be filled with greater glory and where the people will experience peace and prosperity.
The chapter reflects on the people's past failures and the divine judgment they have faced due to their neglect.
God promises a new era of blessing and fruitfulness beginning from the day the temple foundation was laid.
The chapter begins with a call for the people to return to God, emphasizing past disobedience and the need for repentance.
God expresses deep jealousy for Jerusalem and compassion for His people, contrasting His anger with the nations.
A vision of horses and angels is described, symbolizing God's watchfulness over the land and His judgment.
God announces His intention to rebuild Jerusalem and show mercy, indicating a future restoration.
The chapter describes the scattering of Judah by four horns and the subsequent defeat of these horns by four craftsmen, symbolizing divine judgment against those who oppressed Israel.
The vision of a man measuring Jerusalem and the declaration that it will be filled with people and livestock, followed by divine protection, signals a promise of renewal and security.

themes.theme: Scattering and Return of the People
themes.what: God announces the scattering of the people to the four winds and a call to flee from Babylon, indicating both judgment and the eventual return of the exiled.
The Lord declares his presence among the people, his glory within Jerusalem, and his sending of judgment on those who have plundered Israel, affirming his covenantal commitment.
Joshua the high priest is depicted in soiled garments and is cleansed and clothed in festive attire by divine command.
Joshua faces the adversary but is defended by the Lord, who rebukes the accuser.
The Lord promises to bring a future leader, the 'Sprout,' and to remove the guilt of the land.
A vision of a future time of peace and abundance is given, where people live securely under the vine and fig tree.

themes.theme: A vision of a golden lampstand
themes.what: The chapter begins with a vision of a golden lampstand with seven lamps and two olive trees, which the prophet does not initially understand.

themes.theme: God's power and the rebuilding of the temple
themes.what: God reassures Zerubbabel that the rebuilding of the temple will succeed not by human strength but by the Spirit of God.
God emphasizes that even small beginnings should not be despised, as they are part of His plan and will lead to completion.

themes.theme: The identity of the olive trees
themes.what: The prophet seeks clarification about the two olive trees, which are identified as two sons of Oil who serve the Lord of the whole earth.
The chapter describes a flying scroll representing God's law, which brings death to thieves and false swearers.
A basket containing a guilty woman is shown as a symbol of iniquity being removed from the land.

themes.theme: Transportation of guilt to a distant place
themes.what: The basket with guilt is carried by winged beings to a location in Shinar, where it will be set on a foundation.
The prophet sees four chariots with different colored horses representing the four winds of the heavens, which patrol the earth and are under the authority of the Lord of the whole earth.
The angel explains that the black horses going north signify that God has laid to rest His spirit in the northern land, indicating divine activity or presence there.
The Lord instructs the prophet to take silver and gold from exiles and make crowns for the high priest Joshua, symbolizing a divine promise and restoration.
A vision of a future leader named 'a shoot' who will build the temple and rule with a priest, symbolizing a new era of peace and divine order.
The Lord questions the people's fasting in the fifth and seventh months, pointing out it has no spiritual meaning for Him.
The Lord recalls the earlier prophets' messages when Jerusalem was at peace, which the people ignored.
The people hardened their hearts and refused to listen to the Lord's teachings through the prophets.
The Lord announces judgment, scattering the people and leaving the land desolate.
The chapter describes God's promise to return to Jerusalem and dwell among His people, transforming the city into a place of truth and holiness.
God promises a future of peace, prosperity, and divine blessing for the remnant of His people, including the land and its produce.
The chapter calls the people to live with truth, justice, and peace, warning against deceit and evil intentions.
God declares that He will no longer judge the people as He did in the past, but will instead bring restoration and salvation.
The chapter envisions a future where people from many nations will come to Jerusalem to seek the LORD and His presence.
The chapter announces the coming judgment of the LORD on various cities in the region, including Tyre, Sidon, Ashkelon, Gaza, and Ekron.
It promises a future time of peace, the coming of a righteous and humble king, and the cessation of war.
The chapter speaks of the release of prisoners through the covenant and a promise of restoration and doubling of blessings.
The LORD is depicted as a warrior who will intervene powerfully, using lightning, trumpet, and storms to protect and deliver His people.
The chapter concludes with a vision of future abundance and joy, with grain and wine in abundance for the people.
The chapter begins with a call to seek rain from God, highlighting His role in providing for the land, and shifts to judgment on false prophets and leaders who have failed the people.
God promises to restore and strengthen the tribes of Judah and Joseph, showing His compassion and commitment to His people.
The people are depicted as becoming strong and united under God, with their descendants rejoicing in His presence.
The chapter begins with vivid imagery of destruction, symbolizing divine judgment on the land and its people.
The prophet is commanded to act as a shepherd to a doomed flock, illustrating the failure of leadership and divine abandonment.
The prophet symbolically breaks two staffs, representing the breaking of the covenant with the nations and the unity between Judah and Israel.
The chapter concludes with a prophecy of a foolish and destructive shepherd who will abandon and exploit the people.

themes.theme: Jerusalem as a target of siege
themes.what: The chapter describes Jerusalem being surrounded and attacked by all the peoples around it.
God promises to defend Jerusalem and to strike down the enemies of Judah and their forces.
